questions.q: The radius of gyration of a solid sphere of mass 5 kg about $X Y$ is 5 m as shown in figure. The radius of the sphere is $\frac{5 x}{\sqrt{7}} \mathrm{~m}$, then the value of $x$ is:
questions.solution:
$I_{X Y}=I_{C M}+M R^2=\frac{2}{5} M R^2+M R^2=\frac{7}{5} M R^2=\frac{7}{5} \times 5 R^2=7 R^2$...(1)
$I_{X Y}=M K^2=5 \times 5^2$...(ii)
$\therefore 5 \times 5^2=7 \times R^2 \quad[$ From (1) and (2)]
$\Rightarrow R=\sqrt{\frac{5}{7}} \times 5=\frac{5 x}{\sqrt{7}} \quad$ (Given)
$\therefore x=\sqrt{5}$

questions.q: The ratio of radius of gyration of a solid sphere of mass $M$ and radius $R$ about its own axis to the radius of gyration of the thin hollow sphere of same mass and radius about its axis is :
questions.solution:
Radius of gyration of solid sphere about its own axis is given by,

${k}_{solid} = \sqrt{\dfrac{I}{M}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{\dfrac{2M{R}^{2}}{5}}{M}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2}{5}}R$

Similarly,

${k}_{hollow} = \sqrt{\dfrac{I}{M}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{\dfrac{2M{R}^{2}}{3}}{M}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2}{3}}R$

Therefore, required ratio would be

$\dfrac{{k}_{solid}}{{k}_{hollow}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{3}{5}}$.

Note: This option was not present in the original paper.

questions.q: An energy of $484 \mathrm{~J}$ is spent in increasing the speed of a flywheel from $60 \mathrm{rpm}$ to $360 \mathrm{rpm}$. The moment of inertia of the flywheel is:
questions.solution:
Given,
$\begin{aligned}
& \omega_1=60 \mathrm{rpm}=60 \times \frac{2 \pi}{60}=2 \pi \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s} \\
& \omega_2=360 \mathrm{rpm}=360 \times \frac{2 \pi}{60}=12 \pi \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s}
\end{aligned}$
Change in kinetic energy,
$\begin{aligned}
\Delta \mathrm{K} . \mathrm{E} & =\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{I}\left(\omega_2^2-\omega_1^2\right) \\
484 & =\frac{1}{2} \times \mathrm{I}\left(\omega_2+\omega_1\right)\left(\omega_2-\omega_1\right) \\
\Rightarrow \quad \mathrm{I} & =\frac{484 \times 2}{14 \pi \times 10 \pi}=0.7 \mathrm{~kg} \cdot \mathrm{m}^2
\end{aligned}$
(where, the symbols have their usual meanings)

questions.q: A solid sphere $A$ of radius $R$ and mass $M$ is attached at a point to a smaller solid sphere $B$ of radius $r < R$ and mass $m < M$. Assume that the line joining their centres lies along the horizontal. The moment of inertia of the system calculated about a vertical axis passing through the centre of $A$ is $I_A$ and that calculated about a vertical axis passing through the centre of $B$ is $I_B$. The difference $I_A-I_B$ is :
questions.solution:
The distance between the centres of the two spheres $A$ and $B$ is $d = R + r$.

Let $I_{A,\text{cm}}$ and $I_{B,\text{cm}}$ be the moments of inertia of spheres $A$ and $B$ about their respective vertical centroidal axes. For solid spheres, $I_{A,\text{cm}} = \dfrac{2}{5}MR^2$ and $I_{B,\text{cm}} = \dfrac{2}{5}mr^2$.

The moment of inertia of the system about a vertical axis passing through the centre of $A$ is given by the sum of the moment of inertia of $A$ about its own centre and the moment of inertia of $B$ about the centre of $A$. Using the parallel axis theorem:
$I_A = I_{A,\text{cm}} + \left[ I_{B,\text{cm}} + m(R+r)^2 \right]$

Similarly, the moment of inertia of the system about a vertical axis passing through the centre of $B$ is:
$I_B = \left[ I_{A,\text{cm}} + M(R+r)^2 \right] + I_{B,\text{cm}}$

Now, finding the difference $I_A - I_B$:
$I_A - I_B = \left( I_{A,\text{cm}} + I_{B,\text{cm}} + m(R+r)^2 \right) - \left( I_{A,\text{cm}} + M(R+r)^2 + I_{B,\text{cm}} \right)$

$I_A - I_B = m(R+r)^2 - M(R+r)^2$

$I_A - I_B = (m - M)(R+r)^2$

Answer: $(m-M)(R+r)^2$

questions.q: The angular speed of a flywheel is increased from $600$ rpm to $1200$ rpm in $10$ s. The number of revolutions completed by the flywheel during this time is :
questions.solution:
Initial angular speed, $\omega_0 = \dfrac{600 \times 2\pi}{60} = 20\pi$ rad/s

Final angular speed, $\omega = \dfrac{1200 \times 2\pi}{60} = 40\pi$ rad/s

Angular acceleration, $\alpha = \dfrac{\omega - \omega_0}{t} = \dfrac{40\pi - 20\pi}{10} = 2\pi$ rad/s$^2$

Angular displacement, $\theta = \omega_0 t + \dfrac{1}{2}\alpha t^2$

$\theta = 20\pi \times 10 + \dfrac{1}{2} \times 2\pi \times (10)^2 = 200\pi + 100\pi = 300\pi$ rad

Number of revolutions, $N = \dfrac{\theta}{2\pi} = \dfrac{300\pi}{2\pi} = 150$

Answer: $150$

questions.q: From a circular ring of mass $M$ and radius $R$ an arc corresponding to a $90 °$ sector is removed. The moment of inertia of the remaining part of the ring about an axis passing through the centre of the ring and perpendicular to the plane of the ring is  $K$ times $M{R}^{2}$. Then the value of  $K$ is___
questions.solution:
mass per unit length of the ring is

$\lambda = \dfrac{M}{2\piR}$

Moment of inertia of remaining part is

${I}^{'} = {M}^{'}{R}^{2} = \dfrac{3}{4}M{R}^{2} = KM{R}^{2}$

$∴ K = \dfrac{3}{4}$

questions.q: A uniform rod of length $200cm$ and mass $500g$ is balanced on a wedge placed at $40cm$ mark. A mass of $2kg$ is suspended from the rod at $20cm$ and another unknown mass $m$ is suspended from the rod at $160cm$ mark as shown in the figure. Find the value of $m$ such that the rod is in equilibrium. $\left( g = 10m{s}^{- 2}\right)$
questions.solution:
Balancing torque about the wedge, we get

$2g \times 20 = 0 . 5g \times 60 + mg \times 120$

$⇒ 2 = 1 . 5 + 6m$

$⇒ m = \dfrac{0 . 5}{6} = \dfrac{1}{12}kg$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A solid cylinder of mass $2 \mathrm{~kg}$ and radius $50 \mathrm{~cm}$ rolls up an inclined plane of angle inclination $30^{\circ}$. The centre of mass of cylinder has speed of $4 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$. The distance travelled by the cylinder on the inclined surface will be : (Take $g=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2$ )
questions.solution:
When a body rolls i.e. have rotational motion, the total kinetic energy of the system will be $$ \mathrm{KE}=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{mv}^2\left(1+\frac{\mathrm{k}^2}{\mathrm{R}^2}\right) $$ where, $\mathrm{m}=$ mass of body, $\mathrm{v}=$ velocity and $\mathrm{k}=$ radius of gyration
Given, $\mathrm{m}=2 \mathrm{~kg}, \theta=30^{\circ}, \mathrm{v}=4 $$\mathrm{~ms}^{-1}$$ Let $h$ be the height of the inclined plane, then from law of conservation of energy, $$ \begin{aligned} \mathrm{KE} & =\mathrm{PE} \\ \frac{1}{2} \mathrm{mv}^2\left(1+\frac{\mathrm{k}^2}{\mathrm{R}^2}\right) & =\mathrm{mgh} \end{aligned} $$ Substituting the given values in the above equation, we get $$ \begin{aligned} & \frac{1}{2} \times 2 \times 16\left(1+\frac{1}{2}\right)=2 \times 10 \times \mathrm{h}\left[\because \text{ For cylinder } \frac{\mathrm{k}^2}{\mathrm{R}^2}=\frac{1}{2}\right] \\ & \Rightarrow \quad 8 \times \frac{3}{2}=10 \mathrm{~h} \Rightarrow \mathrm{h}=1.2 \mathrm{~m} \end{aligned} $$ From the above diagram $$ \begin{gathered} \sin \theta=\frac{\mathrm{h}}{\mathrm{x}} \\ \Rightarrow \mathrm{x}=\frac{\mathrm{h}}{\sin \theta}=\frac{1.2}{\sin 30^{\circ}}=1.2 \times 2=2.4 \mathrm{~m}\left[\because \sin 30^{\circ}=\frac{1}{2}\right] \end{gathered} $

questions.q: Find the torque about the origin when a force of $3\overset{^}{j}N$ acts on a particle whose position vector is $2\overset{^}{k}m$.
questions.solution:
$\overset{\to}{F} = 3\overset{^}{j}N, \overset{\to}{r} = 2\overset{^}{k}$

$\overset{\to}{τ} = \overset{\to}{r} \times \overset{\to}{F} = 2\overset{^}{k} \times 3\overset{^}{j} = 6 ( \overset{^}{k} \times \overset{^}{j} )$

$= 6 ( - \overset{^}{i} )$

$\overset{\to}{τ} = - 6\overset{^}{i}Nm$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A rope is wound around a hollow cylinder of mass $3 kg$ and radius $40 cm.$ What is the angular acceleration of the cylinder if the rope is pulled with a force of $30 N$?
questions.solution:
The torque about centre is $τ = I\alpha$, here $I$ is the moment of inertia and $\alpha$ is angular acceleration.

The formula of moment of inertia is $M{R}^{2}$.

$F \times R = M{R}^{2}\alpha$

$30 \times 0.4 = 3 \times {\left(0.4\right)}^{2}\alpha$

$12 = 3 \times 0.16\alpha$

$400 = 16\alpha$

Thus, angular acceleration is $\alpha = 25rad / {s}^{2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two discs of same moment of inertia $( I ) $ are rotating in same sense about their regular axis passing through centre and perpendicular to the plane of disc with angular velocities ${\omega}_{1}$ and ${\omega}_{2}$. They are brought into contact face to face coinciding the axis of rotation. The expression for loss in energy during this process is
questions.solution:
The initial angular momentum of two discs is ${I}_{1}{\omega}_{1} + {I}_{2}{\omega}_{2} = I\left({\omega}_{1} + {\omega}_{2}\right)$.

The final angular momentum of system is $\left({I}_{1} + {I}_{2}\right)\omega = 2I\omega$

From the conservation of angular momentum, $\omega = \dfrac{{\omega}_{1} + {\omega}_{2}}{2}$.

Initial kinetic energy, $K{E}_{i} = \dfrac{1}{2}I\left({\omega}_{1}^{2} + {\omega}_{2}^{2}\right)$

and final kinetic energy, $K{E}_{f} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(2I\right)\dfrac{{\left({\omega}_{1} + {\omega}_{2}\right)}^{2}}{4}$

Loss in kinetic energy is $\DeltaKE = \dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{{I}_{1}{I}_{2}}{{I}_{1} + {I}_{2}}{\left({\omega}_{1} - {\omega}_{2}\right)}^{2}$

$= \dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{{I}^{2}}{\left(2I\right)}{\left({\omega}_{1} - {\omega}_{2}\right)}^{2}$

$= \dfrac{1}{4}I{\left({\omega}_{1} - {\omega}_{2}\right)}^{2}$

and final kinetic energy, $K{E}_{f} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(2I\right)\dfrac{{\left({\omega}_{1} + {\omega}_{2}\right)}^{2}}{4}$

Loss in kinetic energy is $\DeltaKE = \dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{{I}_{1}{I}_{2}}{{I}_{1} + {I}_{2}}{\left({\omega}_{1} - {\omega}_{2}\right)}^{2}$

$= \dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{{I}^{2}}{\left(2I\right)}{\left({\omega}_{1} - {\omega}_{2}\right)}^{2}$

$= \dfrac{1}{4}I{\left({\omega}_{1} - {\omega}_{2}\right)}^{2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A thin wire of length '$L$' and linear mass density '$m$' is bent into a circular ring (in $x$-$y$ plane) with centre '$C$' as shown in figure. The moment of inertia of the ring about an axis $yy'$ will be :
questions.solution:
Total mass of the ring, $M = m L$.

Since the wire of length $L$ is bent into a circular ring of radius $R$, its circumference is $L$.

$2\pi R = L \Rightarrow R = \dfrac{L}{2\pi}$

The axis $yy'$ is a tangent to the ring in its plane. The moment of inertia of a ring about its diametric axis is $I_{d} = \dfrac{1}{2}MR^2$.

Using the parallel axis theorem, the moment of inertia of the ring about the tangent $yy'$ is:

$I_{yy'} = I_{d} + MR^2$

$I_{yy'} = \dfrac{1}{2}MR^2 + MR^2 = \dfrac{3}{2}MR^2$

Substituting the values of $M$ and $R$:

$I_{yy'} = \dfrac{3}{2}(mL)\left(\dfrac{L}{2\pi}\right)^2$

$I_{yy'} = \dfrac{3}{2}mL \left(\dfrac{L^2}{4\pi^2}\right)$

$I_{yy'} = \dfrac{3mL^3}{8\pi^2}$

Answer: $\dfrac{3\ mL^{3}}{8\pi^{2}}$

questions.q: A small object of uniform density rolls up a curved surface with an initial velocity $v^{\prime}$. It reaches up to a maximum height of $\frac{3 v^2}{4 g}$ with respect to the initial position. The object is
questions.solution:
As $v=\sqrt{\frac{2 g h}{1+\frac{k^2}{r^2}}}$
Given $h=\frac{3 v^2}{4 g}$
$v^2=\frac{2 g h}{1+\frac{k^2}{r^2}}=\frac{2 g 3 v^2}{4 g\left(1+\frac{k^2}{r^2}\right)}=\frac{6 g v^2}{4 g\left(1+\frac{u^2}{v^2}\right)}$
$1=\frac{3}{2\left(1+\frac{k^2}{v^2}\right)}$
or $1+\frac{k^2}{r^2}=\frac{3}{2}$ or $\frac{k^2}{r^2}=\frac{3}{2}-1=\frac{1}{2}$
$k^2=\frac{1}{2} r^2$ (Equation of disc)
Hence, the object is disc.

questions.q: A solid sphere is in rolling motion. In rolling motion a body possesses translational kinetic energy $\left({K}_{t}\right)$ as well as rotational kinetic energy $\left({K}_{r}\right)$ simultaneously. The ratio ${K}_{t}: \left({K}_{t} + {K}_{r}\right) for the sphere is$
questions.solution:
Transnational $KE$ $= \dfrac{1}{2} m{v}^{2}$
Translational $KE +$ Rotational $KE$
$= \dfrac{1}{2} m{v}^{2} + \dfrac{1}{2} I{\omega}^{2}$
$= \dfrac{1}{2} m{v}^{2} + \dfrac{1}{2} ( \dfrac{2}{5} m{r}^{2} ){\omega}^{2}$
$∵$ for rolling motion $v = r\omega$
$= \dfrac{1}{2} m{v}^{2} + \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{2}{5} m{r}^{2} {( \dfrac{v}{r} )}^{2} = \dfrac{7}{10} m{v}^{2}$
So, $\dfrac{{K}_{t}}{{K}_{t} + {K}_{r}} = \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{2} m{v}^{2}}{\dfrac{7}{10} m{v}^{2}} = \dfrac{5}{7}$

questions.q: The ratio of the radii of gyration of a circular disc to that of a circular ring, each of same mass and radius, around their respective axes is
questions.solution:
Key Idea : The square root of the ratio of the moment of inertia of a rigid body and its mass is called radius of gyration.
As in key idea, radius of gyration is given by
$K=\sqrt{\frac{I}{M}}$
For given problem
$\frac{K_{\text{disc }}}{K_{\text{ring }}}=\sqrt{\frac{I_{\text{disc }}}{I_{\text{ring }}}}$
But $I_{\text{disc }}$ (about its axis) $=\frac{1}{2} M R^2$ and $I_{\text{ring }}$ (about its axis) $=M R^2$ where $R$ is the radius of both bodies. Therefore, Eq. (i) becomes
$\frac{K_{\mathrm{disc}}}{K_{\text{ring }}}=\sqrt{\frac{\frac{1}{2} M R^2}{M R^2}}=1: \sqrt{2}$

questions.q: A solid cylinder of mass $50kg$ and radius $0.5m$ is free to rotate about horizontal axis. A massless string is wound round the cylinder with one end attached to it and other hanging freely. Tension in the string required to produce an angular acceleration of $2$ revolutions ${s}^{- 2}$
questions.solution:
In this question we have to calculate tension

Given M = 50 kg

R = 0.5 m

angular acceleration = 2 revolution/${s}^{2}$

Now, Balancing the Torque

$\left(T\right) \times \left(R\right) = \left(\dfrac{M{R}^{2}}{2}\right)\left(\alpha\right)$

$T = \left(\dfrac{MR}{2}\right)\left(\alpha\right) = \left(\dfrac{50 \times 0.5}{2}\right)\left(2 \times 2\pi\right) = 157N$

So, the tension will be 157 N

questions.q: A solid cylinder of mass $M$ and radius $R$ rolls without slipping on an inclined plane of length $L$ and height $h$. What is the speed of its centre of mass when the cylinder reaches its bottom?
questions.solution:
Here K.E. of centre of mass when cylinder reached the bottom $=\frac{1}{2} m v^2+\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{I} \omega^2 \ldots(\mathrm{i})$
Here $\mathrm{I}=\frac{1}{2} M K^2$ and $\omega=\frac{V}{R}$
$\begin{aligned}
& \therefore \mathrm{KE}=\frac{1}{2} m v^2+\frac{1}{2} M K^2 \cdot \frac{V^2}{r^2} \\
& =\frac{1}{2} m v^2\left[1+\frac{K^2}{R^2}\right]
\end{aligned}$
But for solid cylinder $K=\frac{R}{\sqrt{2}}$ or $\frac{K^2}{R^2}=\frac{1}{2}$
$\therefore K E=\frac{3}{4} m v^2$
PE of the solid cylinder at height $h$ is
$\mathrm{PE}=m g h$
From eq. (ii) and (iii)
$\begin{aligned}
& m g h=\frac{3}{4} m v^2 \\
& \Rightarrow v=\sqrt{\frac{4}{3} g h}
\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A thin horizontal disc is rotating about a vertical axis passing through its fixed centre $O$. Its angular momentum is $L_A$ and $L_B$ computed about points $A$ and $B$, respectively, with $OB=2\times OA$. The value of $\dfrac{L_A}{L_B}$ is :
questions.solution:
The angular momentum of a rigid body about any arbitrary point $P$ is given by the relation:

$\vec{L}_P = \vec{L}_{cm} + \vec{r}_{cm/P} \times M\vec{v}_{cm}$

where $\vec{L}_{cm}$ is the angular momentum of the body about its center of mass, $\vec{r}_{cm/P}$ is the position vector of the center of mass with respect to point $P$, $M$ is the total mass of the body, and $\vec{v}_{cm}$ is the velocity of the center of mass.

In the given problem, the disc is rotating about a vertical axis passing through its fixed center $O$. Since the center of mass of the disc is at $O$ and is fixed, its velocity is zero, i.e., $\vec{v}_{cm} = 0$.

Substituting $\vec{v}_{cm} = 0$ into the angular momentum equation, we get:

$\vec{L}_P = \vec{L}_{cm} + \vec{r}_{cm/P} \times 0$

$\vec{L}_P = \vec{L}_{cm}$

This shows that the angular momentum of the disc is independent of the choice of the reference point and is equal to its angular momentum about the center of mass.

Therefore, the angular momentum about point $A$ is equal to the angular momentum about point $B$:

$L_A = L_B = L_{cm}$

Hence, the ratio is:

$\dfrac{L_A}{L_B} = 1$

Answer: $1$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A thin uniform rod, pivoted at $O$, is rotating in the horizontal plane with constant angular speed $\omega$, as shown in the figure. At time $t=0$, a small insect starts from $O$ and moves with constant speed $v$, with respect to the rod towards the other end. It reaches the end of the rod at $t=T$ and stops. The angular speed of the system remains $\omega$ throughout. The magnitude of the torque $(|\vec{\tau}|)$ about $O$, as a function of time is best represented by which plot?
questions.solution:
Angular momentum, $|\mathbf{L}|$ or $L=I \omega$ (about axis of rod) Moment of inertia of the rod-insect system. $I=I_{\text{rod }}+m x^{2}=I_{\text{rod }}+m v^{2} t^{2}$ Here, $m=$ mass of insect $\therefore \quad L=\left(I_{\mathrm{rod}}+m v^{2} t^{2}\right) \omega$



Now $|\tau|=\frac{d L}{d t}=\left(2 m v^{2} t \omega\right)$ or $|\tau| \propto t$

i.e. the graph is straight line passing through origin.

After time $T, L=$ constant

$\therefore \quad|\tau| \text{ or } \frac{d L}{d t}=0$

i.e., when the insect stops moving, $L$ does not change and therefore $T$ becomes constant.

questions.q: A uniform rod of length $l$ is being rotated in a horizontal plane with a constant angular speed about an axis passing through one of its ends. If the tension generated in the rod due to rotation is $T ( x )$ at a distance $x$ from the axis, then which of the following graphs depicts it most closely?
questions.solution:
The mass of the rod at a distance $x$ from the axis is $dm = \dfrac{M}{L} . dx$
$T = ( dm ) {\omega}^{2}x$

Integrating the above equation from $x$ to $L$
$= {∫}_{x}^{L}\dfrac{M}{L}{\omega}^{2}xdx$
$= \dfrac{M}{L}{\omega}^{2}{\left[\dfrac{{x}^{2}}{2}\right]}_{x}^{L}$
$\dfrac{M}{2L}{\omega}^{2}\left[{L}^{2} - {x}^{2}\right]$
The above equation depicts the relation between tension and length of rod as downward opening parabola.

Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion A and the other is labelled as Reason R.

Assertion A: Moment of inertia of a circular disc of mass $M$ and radius $R$ about $X, Y$ axes (passing through its plane) and Z-axis which is perpendicular to its plane were found to be ${I}_{x}, {I}_{y}$ and ${I}_{z}$, respectively. The respective radii of gyration about all the three axes will be the same.

Reason R: A rigid body making rotational motion has fixed mass and shape. In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both A and R are correct but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is not correct but R is correct.
A is correct but R is not correct.

Both A and R are correct and R is the correct
explanation of A.
questions.solution:
${I}_{z} = {I}_{x} + {I}_{y}$ (using perpendicular axis theorem)

and $I = m{k}^{2} ( K:$ radius of gyration) 

so $m{K}_{z}^{2} = m{K}_{x}^{2} + m{K}_{y}^{2}$

${K}_{z}^{2} = {K}_{x}^{2} + {K}_{y}^{2}$

So radius of gyration about axes $x, y$ and $z$ will not be same, hence assertion A is not correct reason R is correct statement (property of a rigid body).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Statement 1 Two cylinders, one hollow (metal) and the other solid (wood) with the same mass and identical dimensions are simultaneously allowed to roll without slipping down an inclined plane from the same height. The hollow cylinder will reach the bottom of the inclined plane first.
and Statement 2 By the principle of conservation of energy, the total kinetic energies of both the cylinders are identical when they reach the bottom of the incline.
options: Statement 1 is true, Statement 2 is true, Statement 2 is a correct explanation for Statement 1.
Statement 1 is true, Statement 2 is true, Statement 2 is not a correct explanation for Statement 1.
Statement 1 is true, Statement 2 is false.
Statement 1 is false, Statement 2 is true
questions.solution:
In case of pure rolling on inclined plane,
$\begin{aligned}
& a=\frac{g \sin \theta}{1+I / m R^2} \\
& I_{\text{solid }} < I_{\text{hollow }} \\
\therefore \quad & a_{\text{solid }}>a_{\text{hollow }}
\end{aligned} \therefore$ solid cylinder will reach the bottom first.
Further, in case of pure rolling on stationary ground, work done by friction is zero. Therefore, mechanical energy of both the cylinders will remain constant.
$\begin{aligned}
& \therefore(\mathrm{KE})_{\text{Hollow }}=(\mathrm{KE})_{\text{solid }}=\text{ decrease in } \mathrm{PE}=m g h \\
& \therefore \text{ correct option is }(\mathrm{d})
\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
The torque T on a body about a given point is found to be equal to \(\mathrm{A} \times \mathrm{L}\) where A is constant vector, and \(L\) is the angular momentum of the body about that point. From this it follows that
(A) \(\frac{\mathrm{dL}}{\mathrm{dt}}\) is perpendicular to L at all instants of time
(B) the component of L in the direction of A does not change with time.
(C) the magnitude of L does not change with time.
(D) L does not change with time
questions.solution:
\($\frac{\mathrm{E}}{\mathrm{\tau}}=\frac{\mathrm{d} \mathrm{~L}^{\prime}}{\mathrm{dt}}$\)
Given that
\(\hat{$\mathrm{t}$}=\ddot{$\mathrm{A}$} $\times \ddot{\mathrm{L}} \Rightarrow \frac{\mathrm{dL}}{\mathrm{dt}}=\stackrel{\|}{\mathrm{A}} \times \stackrel{\mathbb{X}}{\mathrm{L}}$\)
\($\frac{\mathrm{dL}}{\mathrm{dt}}$\)
From cross-product rule, \($\frac{d L}{d t}$\) is always perpendicular to the plane containing \(A\) and L
By the dot product definition
\(\vec{L} . \vec{L}=L²\)
Differentiating with respect to time
\(\stackrel{$\mathrm{Z}$}{$\mathrm{~L}$} $\cdot \frac{\mathrm{dL}}{\mathrm{dt}}+\stackrel{\mathrm{Z}}{\mathrm{~L}} \cdot \frac{\mathrm{dL}}{\mathrm{dt}}=$2 $\mathrm{~L} \cdot \frac{\mathrm{dL}}{\mathrm{dt}}$\)
\(\Rightarrow \quad 2 L $\cdot \frac{d L}{d t}=$2 L $\frac{d L}{d t}$\)
Since \($\frac{d L}{d t}$\) is perpendicular to \(L \Rightarrow $\frac{d L}{d t}=$0 \Rightarrow L=\) constant
questions.question:

(A) \(\frac{\mathrm{dL}}{\mathrm{dt}}\) is perpendicular to L at all instants of time
(B) the component of L in the direction of A does not change with time.
(C) the magnitude of L does not change with time.
(D) L does not change with time
questions.explanation:
\(\frac{\mathrm{E}}{\mathrm{\tau}}=\frac{\mathrm{d} \mathrm{~L}^{\prime}}{\mathrm{dt}}\)
Given that
\(\hat{\mathrm{t}}=\ddot{\mathrm{A}} \times \ddot{\mathrm{L}} \Rightarrow \frac{\mathrm{dL}}{\mathrm{dt}}=\stackrel{\|}{\mathrm{A}} \times \stackrel{\mathbb{X}}{\mathrm{L}}\)
\(\frac{\mathrm{dL}}{\mathrm{dt}}\)
From cross-product rule, \(\frac{d L}{d t}\) is always perpendicular to the plane containing \(A\) and L
By the dot product definition
\(\vec{L} . \vec{L}=L^2\)
Differentiating with respect to time
\(\stackrel{\mathrm{Z}}{\mathrm{~L}} \cdot \frac{\mathrm{dL}}{\mathrm{dt}}+\stackrel{\mathrm{Z}}{\mathrm{~L}} \cdot \frac{\mathrm{dL}}{\mathrm{dt}}=2 \mathrm{~L} \cdot \frac{\mathrm{dL}}{\mathrm{dt}}\)
\(\Rightarrow \quad 2 L \cdot \frac{d L}{d t}=2 L \frac{d L}{d t}\)
Since \(\frac{d L}{d t}\) is perpendicular to \(L \Rightarrow \frac{d L}{d t}=0 \Rightarrow L=\) constant

questions.q:
Four rods of equal length \(l\) and mass \(m\) each from a square as shown in figure. Moment of inertia about three axes 1,2 and 3 are say \(I_1, I_2\) and \(I_3\). Then, match the following columns \(
Column IColumn II
(A)A_1(P)\tfrac{4}{3} m^2
(B)I_2(q)\tfrac{2}{3} m v^2
(C)I_3(r)\tfrac{1}{2} m m^2
(s)None of the above
\)
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned}
& I_1=2\left(\frac{m l^2}{2}\right) +2(m)\left(\frac{l}{2}\right)^2=\frac{2}{3} m l^2 \\
& I_2=0+2\left(\frac{m l^2}{3}\right)+m l^2=\left(\frac{5}{3}\right) m l^2 \\
& I_3=4\left[\frac{m l^2}{3} \sin ^2 45^{\mathrm{s}}\right]=\frac{2}{3} m l^2=I_1
\end{aligned}\)$

questions.q:
If radius of the earth is reduced to half without changing its mass, then match the following columns \(
Column IColumn II
(A)Angular momentum(p)Will become two times
of the earth
(B)Time period of rotation(a)Will become four times
of the earth
(C)Rotational kinetic energy(r)Will remain constant
of the earth
(s)None of the above
\)
questions.solution:
In the absence of external torque, angular momentum remains constant.
\(\begin{gathered}
L=I \omega=\text{ constant } \\
I \propto R^2
\end{gathered}\)
\(\therefore I\) will remain \(\frac{1}{4}\) th or \(\omega\) will become 4 times.
Therefore, time period (\(T\)) will remain \(\frac{1}{4}\) th
Further,
\(K=\frac{L^2}{2 I}\)
Since, angular momentum is constant and I has become \(\frac{1}{-} \mathrm{th}\).
Therefore, kinetic energy will become 4 times.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A uniform cube of mass \(m\) and side \(a\) is placed on a frictionless horizontal surface. A vertical force \(F\) is applied to the edge as shown in figure. Match the following (most appropriate choice) \(
Column IColumn II
(a)m g/4 < F < m g/2(p)Cube will move up
(b)F > m g/2(q)Cube will not exhibit motion
(c)F > m g(r)Cube will begin to rotate
and slip at A
(d)F = m g/4(s)Normal reaction effectively at a/3 from A,
no motion
\)
questions.solution:
Consider the below diagram

Moment of the force \(F\) about point \(A, \tau_1=F \times a\) (anti-clockwise)
Moment of weight \(m g\) of the cube about point \(A\),
\(\tau_2=m g \times \frac{a}{2} \text{ (clockwise) }\)
Cube will not exhibit motion, if \(\tau_1=\tau_2\)
(\(\because\) In this case, both the torque will cancel the effect of each other]
\(\begin{array}{ll}
\therefore & F \times a=m g \times \frac{a}{2} \\
\Rightarrow & F=\frac{m g}{2}
\end{array}\)
Cube will rotate only when, \(\tau_1>\tau_2\)
\(\Rightarrow \quad F \times a>m g \times \frac{a}{2} \Rightarrow F>\frac{m g}{2}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A uniform sphere of mass \(m\) and radius \(R\) is placed on a rough horizontal surface (figure). The sphere is struck horizontally at a height \(h\) from the floor. Match the following \(
Column IColumn II
(a)h = R/2(p)Sphere rolls without slipping,
with constant velocity and no loss of energy
(b)h = R(q)Sphere spins clockwise, loses energy
by friction
(c)h = 3R/2(r)Sphere spins anti-clockwise, loses energy
by friction
(d)h = 7R/5(s)Sphere has only translational motion,
loses energy by friction
\)
questions.solution:
The sphere will roll without slipping when \(\omega=\frac{v}{r}\), where \(v\) is linear velocity and \(\omega\) is angular velocity of the sphere. Now, angular momentum of sphere, about centre of mass [We are applying conservation of angular momentum just before and after struck]
$\begin{aligned}
m v(h-R) & =I \omega=\left(\frac{2}{5} m R^2\right)\left(\frac{v}{R}\right) \\
m v(h-R) & =\frac{2}{5} m v R \\
h-R & =\frac{2}{5} R \Rightarrow h=\frac{7}{5} R
\end{aligned}\)
Therefore,$ the $sphere will roll without slipping with a constant velocity and hence, no loss of energy, so \(\quad D \rightarrow p\) Torque due to applied force, \(F\) about centre of mass
\(\tau=F(h-R)\) (clockwise)
For \(\tau=0, h=R\), sphere will have only translational motion. It would lose energy by friction.
Hence,
\(\mathrm{B} \rightarrow \mathrm{~s}\)
The sphere will spin clockwise when \(\tau>0 \Rightarrow h>R\)
Therefore, \(C \rightarrow q\)
The sphere will spin anti-clockwise when
\(\tau < 0 \Rightarrow h < R, \Lambda \rightarrow \mathrm{r}\)$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A uniform rod of mass $M$ and length $L$ is hinged at one of its ends. It is held in a horizontal position and then released from rest. The angular speed of the rod when it reaches the lowest (vertical) position is:
questions.solution:
When the rod moves from the horizontal to the vertical position, its center of mass falls by a distance $h = \dfrac{L}{2}$.

The loss in gravitational potential energy is:
$\Delta U = Mg\left(\dfrac{L}{2}\right)$

This loss in potential energy is converted into rotational kinetic energy. The moment of inertia of a uniform rod about an axis through its end is $I = \dfrac{ML^2}{3}$.

Gain in rotational kinetic energy:
$\Delta K = \dfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{ML^2}{3}\right)\omega^2$

By conservation of mechanical energy:
$Mg\left(\dfrac{L}{2}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{ML^2}{3}\right)\omega^2$
$MgL = \dfrac{ML^2}{3}\omega^2$
$\omega^2 = \dfrac{3g}{L}$
$\omega = \sqrt{\dfrac{3g}{L}}$

Assuming the center of mass falls by $L$ incorrectly gives $\sqrt{\dfrac{6g}{L}}$, and using the moment of inertia about the center ($\dfrac{ML^2}{12}$) incorrectly gives $\sqrt{\dfrac{12g}{L}}$.

Answer: $\sqrt{\dfrac{3g}{L}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II regarding the radius of gyration ($k$) of various uniform symmetric bodies of radius $R$.

List-I (Body and Axis)List-II (Radius of Gyration)
A. Thin ring about its diameterI. $\dfrac{R}{2}$
B. Thin uniform disc about its diameterII. $\dfrac{R}{\sqrt{2}}$
C. Solid sphere about its diameterIII. $\sqrt{\dfrac{2}{5}}R$
D. Hollow sphere about its diameterIV. $\sqrt{\dfrac{2}{3}}R$

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
The radius of gyration $k$ is given by $k = \sqrt{\dfrac{I}{M}}$.

A. For a thin ring about its diameter, $I = \dfrac{MR^2}{2} \implies k = \dfrac{R}{\sqrt{2}}$. (Matches II)

B. For a thin uniform disc about its diameter, $I = \dfrac{MR^2}{4} \implies k = \dfrac{R}{2}$. (Matches I)

C. For a solid sphere about its diameter, $I = \dfrac{2}{5}MR^2 \implies k = \sqrt{\dfrac{2}{5}}R$. (Matches III)

D. For a hollow sphere about its diameter, $I = \dfrac{2}{3}MR^2 \implies k = \sqrt{\dfrac{2}{3}}R$. (Matches IV)

Therefore, the correct matching is A-II, B-I, C-III, D-IV.

Answer: A-II, B-I, C-III, D-IV

questions.q: An electric fan with blades of length $0.4 \text{ m}$ starts from rest. It reaches a steady rotational speed of $300 \text{ rpm}$ in $5 \text{ s}$ with uniform angular acceleration. The tangential acceleration of a point at the tip of the blade is:
questions.solution:
Given, initial angular speed $\omega_0 = 0$
Final angular speed $\omega = 300 \text{ rpm}$
Time $t = 5 \text{ s}$
Radius of the circular path of the tip $R = 0.4 \text{ m}$

First, convert the final angular speed into $\text{rad s}^{-1}$:
$\omega = 300 \times \dfrac{2\pi}{60} \text{ rad s}^{-1} = 10\pi \text{ rad s}^{-1}$

Calculate the angular acceleration $\alpha$ using the first equation of rotational kinematics:
$\alpha = \dfrac{\omega - \omega_0}{t} = \dfrac{10\pi - 0}{5} = 2\pi \text{ rad s}^{-2}$

The tangential acceleration $a_t$ is related to angular acceleration by the formula:

questions.q: A uniform solid cylinder of mass $M$ and radius $R$ has a wedge-shaped slice corresponding to a $60^{\circ}$ sector removed along its entire length. The moment of inertia of the remaining portion of the cylinder about its natural geometric axis is
questions.solution:
The angle of the removed sector is $60^{\circ}$.

The angle of the remaining portion of the cylinder is $360^{\circ} - 60^{\circ} = 300^{\circ}$.

Since the cylinder is uniform, the mass is proportional to the sector angle. The mass of the remaining portion $M'$ is:
$M' = \dfrac{300^{\circ}}{360^{\circ}} M = \dfrac{5}{6} M$

The moment of inertia of a solid cylinder (or any sector of it) about its central geometric axis is given by $\dfrac{1}{2} \times \text{mass} \times \text{radius}^2$.

Therefore, the moment of inertia of the remaining portion is:
$I' = \dfrac{1}{2} M' R^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} \left(\dfrac{5}{6} M\right) R^2 = \dfrac{5}{12} M R^2$

Answer: $\dfrac{5}{12}MR^2$

questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): When a person spinning on a frictionless chair pulls their arms inwards, their rotational kinetic energy increases even though no external torque acts on the system.

Reason (R): When the person pulls their arms inwards, the angular momentum of the system increases, leading to an increase in rotational kinetic energy.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.solution:
Assertion (A) is correct: When the person pulls their arms inwards, their moment of inertia ($I$) decreases. Since no external torque acts on the system, angular momentum ($L$) is conserved. The rotational kinetic energy is given by $K = \dfrac{L^2}{2I}$. As $I$ decreases while $L$ remains constant, the rotational kinetic energy $K$ increases. The extra energy comes from the internal work done by the person's muscles.

Reason (R) is incorrect: The angular momentum of the system does not increase; it remains conserved because the net external torque is zero.

Answer: (A) is correct but (R) is not correct

questions.q: Two identical uniform solid spheres, each of mass $M$ and radius $R$, have their centres connected by a light rigid rod of length $2R$. The radius of gyration of this combined system about an axis passing through the centre of the rod and perpendicular to its length is:
questions.solution:
The axis of rotation passes through the centre of the rod of length $2R$. The distance from this axis to the centre of each sphere is $R$.

The moment of inertia of one solid sphere about its own diametric axis is $I_{cm} = \dfrac{2}{5} M R^2$.
Using the parallel axis theorem, the moment of inertia of one sphere about the given axis of rotation is:
$I_{sphere} = I_{cm} + M d^2 = \dfrac{2}{5} M R^2 + M R^2 = \dfrac{7}{5} M R^2$

Since there are two identical spheres, the total moment of inertia of the system is:
$I_{system} = 2 \times \dfrac{7}{5} M R^2 = \dfrac{14}{5} M R^2$

The total mass of the system is $M_{total} = 2M$.
Let $K$ be the radius of gyration of the system. Then $I_{system} = M_{total} K^2$.
$\dfrac{14}{5} M R^2 = (2M) K^2$
$K^2 = \dfrac{7}{5} R^2$
$K = \sqrt{\dfrac{7}{5}} R$

Answer: $\sqrt{\dfrac{7}{5}} R$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The torque $\tau$ applied on a rigid body of moment of inertia $2 \text{ kg m}^2$ varies with its angular displacement $\theta$. The graph of $\tau$ versus $\theta$ is a straight line starting from the origin and reaching a maximum torque of $10 \text{ N m}$ at an angular displacement of $20 \text{ rad}$. If the body starts from rest, its final angular speed at $\theta = 20 \text{ rad}$ is:
questions.solution:
The work done on the body is equal to the area under the torque-angular displacement graph.

Since the graph is a triangle starting from the origin:
$\text{Work done } (W) = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height}$
$W = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 20 \text{ rad} \times 10 \text{ N m} = 100 \text{ J}$

According to the work-energy theorem for rotational motion, the work done is equal to the change in rotational kinetic energy:
$W = \Delta K = \dfrac{1}{2} I \omega^2 - 0$
$100 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 2 \times \omega^2$
$\omega^2 = 100 \implies \omega = 10 \text{ rad/s}$

Answer: $10 \text{ rad/s}$

questions.q: A solid cylinder of radius $R_1$ and a solid sphere of radius $R_2$ have the same mass. If their radii of gyration about their respective central axes of symmetry are equal, then the ratio $R_1 : R_2$ is:
questions.solution:
The radius of gyration of a solid cylinder about its central axis is given by $k_{cyl} = \sqrt{\dfrac{I}{M}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{\dfrac{1}{2}MR_1^2}{M}} = \dfrac{R_1}{\sqrt{2}}$.

The radius of gyration of a solid sphere about its central axis is given by $k_{sph} = \sqrt{\dfrac{I}{M}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{\dfrac{2}{5}MR_2^2}{M}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2}{5}}R_2$.

Given that $k_{cyl} = k_{sph}$, we have:
$\dfrac{R_1}{\sqrt{2}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2}{5}}R_2$

$\Rightarrow \dfrac{R_1}{R_2} = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}}$

Thus, the ratio $R_1 : R_2$ is $2 : \sqrt{5}$.

Answer: $2 : \sqrt{5}$

questions.q: A uniform circular disc has mass $M$ and radius $R$. Let $K_1$ be its radius of gyration about an axis passing through its centre and perpendicular to its plane. Let $K_2$ be its radius of gyration about an axis tangential to its edge and lying in the plane of the disc. The ratio $K_1 : K_2$ is:
questions.solution:
The moment of inertia of the disc about an axis passing through its centre and perpendicular to its plane is:
$I_1 = \dfrac{1}{2} M R^2$
Since $I_1 = M K_1^2$, the radius of gyration $K_1$ is:
$K_1 = \dfrac{R}{\sqrt{2}}$

The moment of inertia of the disc about its diameter is $I_d = \dfrac{1}{4} M R^2$.
Using the parallel axis theorem, the moment of inertia about a tangent in the plane of the disc is:
$I_2 = I_d + M R^2 = \dfrac{1}{4} M R^2 + M R^2 = \dfrac{5}{4} M R^2$
Since $I_2 = M K_2^2$, the radius of gyration $K_2$ is:
$K_2 = \dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{2} R$

The ratio $K_1 : K_2$ is:
$\dfrac{K_1}{K_2} = \dfrac{\dfrac{R}{\sqrt{2}}}{\dfrac{\sqrt{5} R}{2}} = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{10}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2}{5}}$

Answer: $\sqrt{\dfrac{2}{5}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The angular momentum of a moving rigid body is measured about several different stationary points in the laboratory frame. It is found that the angular momentum vector is exactly the same about every point. Which of the following statements must be true regarding the motion of the body?
options: The body is undergoing pure translational motion with a constant velocity.
The body is rolling without slipping on a fixed horizontal surface.
The center of mass of the body is stationary.
The body is rotating about a fixed axis that does not pass through its center of mass.
questions.solution:
The angular momentum of a rigid body about any arbitrary stationary point $P$ is given by the relation:

$\vec{L}_P = \vec{L}_{cm} + \vec{r}_{cm/P} \times M\vec{v}_{cm}$

where $\vec{L}_{cm}$ is the angular momentum about the center of mass, $\vec{r}_{cm/P}$ is the position vector of the center of mass with respect to point $P$, $M$ is the mass, and $\vec{v}_{cm}$ is the velocity of the center of mass.

For the angular momentum $\vec{L}_P$ to be exactly the same about every stationary point $P$, the term $\vec{r}_{cm/P} \times M\vec{v}_{cm}$ must be zero for all possible position vectors $\vec{r}_{cm/P}$.

This is only possible if the velocity of the center of mass is zero ($\vec{v}_{cm} = 0$).

Therefore, the center of mass of the body must be stationary. The body can either be completely at rest or in pure rotation about an axis passing through its center of mass.

Answer: The center of mass of the body is stationary.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A rigid body has a radius of gyration $K$ about an axis passing through its centre of mass. The radius of gyration of the body about a parallel axis located at a perpendicular distance $K$ from the centre of mass axis is
questions.solution:
Let the mass of the rigid body be $M$.

The moment of inertia of the body about the axis passing through its centre of mass is $I_{\text{cm}} = MK^2$.

According to the theorem of parallel axes, the moment of inertia $I'$ about a parallel axis at a perpendicular distance $d$ is given by:
$I' = I_{\text{cm}} + Md^2$

Given that the distance $d = K$, we have:
$I' = MK^2 + MK^2 = 2MK^2$

If $K'$ is the new radius of gyration about this parallel axis, then $I' = M(K')^2$.

Equating the two expressions for $I'$:
$M(K')^2 = 2MK^2$
$(K')^2 = 2K^2$
$K' = \sqrt{2}K$.

Answer: $\sqrt{2}K$

questions.q:
A uniform circular ring and a uniform circular disc, both having the same original mass $M$ and radius $R$, have a sector corresponding to an angle of $90^{\circ}$ removed from them. Match the objects in List-I with their respective moments of inertia about an axis passing through their centre and perpendicular to their plane in List-II.

List-IList-II
(A) Remaining part of the ring(I) $\dfrac{3}{4} M R^2$
(B) Remaining part of the disc(II) $\dfrac{3}{8} M R^2$
(C) Removed sector of the ring(III) $\dfrac{1}{4} M R^2$
(D) Removed sector of the disc(IV) $\dfrac{1}{8} M R^2$

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
When a $90^{\circ}$ sector is removed, the fraction of mass removed is $\dfrac{90^{\circ}}{360^{\circ}} = \dfrac{1}{4}$. The fraction of mass remaining is $\dfrac{3}{4}$.

For a ring, the moment of inertia of any sector about the central axis is $I = m R^2$, where $m$ is the mass of that specific sector.
(A) Remaining part of the ring: mass $m = \dfrac{3}{4} M$, so $I = \dfrac{3}{4} M R^2$ (Matches I).
(C) Removed sector of the ring: mass $m = \dfrac{1}{4} M$, so $I = \dfrac{1}{4} M R^2$ (Matches III).

For a disc, the moment of inertia of any sector about the central axis is $I = \dfrac{1}{2} m R^2$.
(B) Remaining part of the disc: mass $m = \dfrac{3}{4} M$, so $I = \dfrac{1}{2} \left(\dfrac{3}{4} M\right) R^2 = \dfrac{3}{8} M R^2$ (Matches II).
(D) Removed sector of the disc: mass $m = \dfrac{1}{4} M$, so $I = \dfrac{1}{2} \left(\dfrac{1}{4} M\right) R^2 = \dfrac{1}{8} M R^2$ (Matches IV).

Therefore, the correct matching is (A)-(I), (B)-(II), (C)-(III), (D)-(IV).

Answer: (A)-(I), (B)-(II), (C)-(III), (D)-(IV)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A medical centrifuge starting from rest is accelerated at a constant uniform rate of $5\pi \text{ rad s}^{-2}$. The time taken by the centrifuge to reach a rotational speed of $3000 \text{ rpm}$ is:
questions.solution:
Given, initial angular speed $\omega_0 = 0$
Angular acceleration $\alpha = 5\pi \text{ rad s}^{-2}$
Final angular speed $\omega = 3000 \text{ rpm}$

First, convert the final angular speed into $\text{rad s}^{-1}$:
$\omega = 3000 \times \dfrac{2\pi}{60} \text{ rad s}^{-1} = 100\pi \text{ rad s}^{-1}$

Using the first equation of rotational kinematics:
$\omega = \omega_0 + \alpha t$
$100\pi = 0 + (5\pi) t$
$t = \dfrac{100\pi}{5\pi} = 20 \text{ s}$

Answer: $20 \text{ s}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A uniform solid spherical planet is rotating about its own axis. Due to geological changes, the planet shrinks uniformly such that its mass remains constant but the length of its day decreases by $36\%$. What is the percentage decrease in the radius of the planet?
questions.solution:
Let the initial time period be $T_i$ and the initial radius be $R_i$.
Since the length of the day decreases by $36\%$, the final time period is:
$T_f = T_i - 0.36 T_i = 0.64 T_i$

By conservation of angular momentum, $I_i \omega_i = I_f \omega_f$.
For a uniform solid sphere, $I = \dfrac{2}{5}MR^2$.
Since $\omega = \dfrac{2\pi}{T}$, we have $\dfrac{R_i^2}{T_i} = \dfrac{R_f^2}{T_f}$.

$\left(\dfrac{R_f}{R_i}\right)^2 = \dfrac{T_f}{T_i} = 0.64$

Taking the square root on both sides:
$\dfrac{R_f}{R_i} = \sqrt{0.64} = 0.8$

This means the final radius is $80\%$ of the initial radius.
The percentage decrease in the radius is:
$\dfrac{R_i - R_f}{R_i} \times 100\% = (1 - 0.8) \times 100\% = 20\%$

Answer: $20\%$

By conservation of angular momentum, $I_i \omega_i = I_f \omega_f$.
For a uniform solid sphere, $I = \dfrac{2}{5}MR^2$.
Since $\omega = \dfrac{2\pi}{T}$, we have $\dfrac{R_i^2}{T_i} = \dfrac{R_f^2}{T_f}$.

$\left(\dfrac{R_f}{R_i}\right)^2 = \dfrac{T_f}{T_i} = 0.64$

Taking the square root on both sides:
$\dfrac{R_f}{R_i} = \sqrt{0.64} = 0.8$

This means the final radius is $80\%$ of the initial radius.
The percentage decrease in the radius is:
$\dfrac{R_i - R_f}{R_i} \times 100\% = (1 - 0.8) \times 100\% = 20\%$

Answer: $20\%$

questions.q: The ratio of the radius of gyration of a uniform solid sphere about an axis tangent to its surface to the radius of gyration of the sphere about its diameter is
questions.solution:
For a uniform solid sphere of mass $M$ and radius $R$:

Moment of inertia about its diameter is $I_{\text{diameter}} = \dfrac{2}{5}MR^2$.
Radius of gyration about the diameter, $k_{\text{diameter}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{I_{\text{diameter}}}{M}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2}{5}}R$.

Using the parallel axis theorem, the moment of inertia about a tangent is $I_{\text{tangent}} = I_{\text{diameter}} + MR^2 = \dfrac{2}{5}MR^2 + MR^2 = \dfrac{7}{5}MR^2$.
Radius of gyration about the tangent, $k_{\text{tangent}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{I_{\text{tangent}}}{M}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{7}{5}}R$.

The required ratio is $\dfrac{k_{\text{tangent}}}{k_{\text{diameter}}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{7/5}R}{\sqrt{2/5}R} = \dfrac{\sqrt{7}}{\sqrt{2}}$.

Answer: $\sqrt{7}:\sqrt{2}$

questions.q: A wheel having a moment of inertia of $2$ kg m$^2$ is rotating at $300$ rpm. It is brought to rest by a constant frictional torque in $25$ revolutions. The magnitude of this frictional torque is :
questions.solution:
Initial angular speed, $\omega_0 = \dfrac{300 \times 2\pi}{60} = 10\pi$ rad/s

Final angular speed, $\omega = 0$

Angular displacement, $\theta = 25 \times 2\pi = 50\pi$ rad

Using the equation of rotational kinematics, $\omega^2 = \omega_0^2 + 2\alpha\theta$

$0 = (10\pi)^2 + 2\alpha(50\pi)$

$\alpha = -\dfrac{100\pi^2}{100\pi} = -\pi$ rad/s$^2$

Magnitude of frictional torque, $\tau = I|\alpha|$

$\tau = 2 \times \pi = 2\pi$ N m

Answer: $2\pi$ N m

questions.q: A uniform thin circular ring of mass $M$ and radius $R$ is cut and a sector of angle $\theta$ is removed. If the moment of inertia of the remaining arc about an axis passing through its centre and perpendicular to its plane is $\dfrac{3}{5}MR^2$, then the value of the removed angle $\theta$ is
questions.solution:
The moment of inertia of a circular arc of mass $m'$ and radius $R$ about its central axis is given by $I = m'R^2$.

Given that the moment of inertia of the remaining arc is $\dfrac{3}{5}MR^2$, we can write:
$m'R^2 = \dfrac{3}{5}MR^2$
$\Rightarrow m' = \dfrac{3}{5}M$

This means the mass of the remaining arc is $\dfrac{3}{5}$ of the original mass. The mass of the removed sector must therefore be:
$m_{\text{removed}} = M - \dfrac{3}{5}M = \dfrac{2}{5}M$

For a uniform ring, the mass of a sector is directly proportional to the angle it subtends at the centre. Thus, the angle $\theta$ of the removed sector is:
$\theta = \dfrac{2}{5} \times 360^{\circ} = 144^{\circ}$

Answer: $144^{\circ}$

questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The radius of gyration of a rigid body of a given shape and size is independent of its total mass, but depends on the position of the axis of rotation.
Reason (R): The radius of gyration is defined as the arithmetic mean of the perpendicular distances of all the constituent particles of the body from the axis of rotation.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false but Reason (R) is true.
questions.solution:
The moment of inertia of a rigid body is given by $I = MK^2$, where $M$ is the total mass and $K$ is the radius of gyration. For a given shape, size, and axis of rotation, $I$ is directly proportional to $M$. Therefore, $K = \sqrt{\dfrac{I}{M}}$ depends only on the mass distribution (geometry) and the position of the axis of rotation, and is independent of the total mass. Thus, Assertion (A) is true.

By definition, the radius of gyration is the root mean square (RMS) distance of the constituent particles from the axis of rotation, not the simple arithmetic mean. For a body made of $n$ particles of equal mass $m$, $K = \sqrt{\dfrac{r_1^2 + r_2^2 + \dots + r_n^2}{n}}$. Thus, Reason (R) is false.

Answer: Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false.

questions.q:
Match List-I with List-II regarding the angular momentum of various rigid bodies.

Let $L_C$ be the magnitude of angular momentum of the body about its centre of mass and $L_P$ be the magnitude of its angular momentum about a stationary point on the ground.

List-I (Object and its motion)List-II (Relation)
A. A disc rotating about a fixed vertical axis passing through its centre of massI. $L_P = 3 L_C$
B. A uniform ring rolling without slipping on a horizontal surfaceII. $L_P = L_C$
C. A uniform solid cylinder rolling without slipping on a horizontal surfaceIII. $L_P = \dfrac{7}{2} L_C$
D. A uniform solid sphere rolling without slipping on a horizontal surfaceIV. $L_P = 2 L_C$

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
The angular momentum about a point $P$ on the ground is $\vec{L}_P = \vec{L}_C + \vec{r}_{cm} \times M\vec{v}_{cm}$.

For a body rotating about a fixed axis through its centre of mass, $\vec{v}_{cm} = 0$. Hence, $L_P = L_C$. This matches A with II.

For a body rolling without slipping on a horizontal surface, $v_{cm} = \omega R$. Both spin and orbital angular momentum are in the same direction.
$L_P = I_{cm}\omega + Mv_{cm}R = I_{cm}\left(\dfrac{v_{cm}}{R}\right) + Mv_{cm}R$

For a ring, $I_{cm} = MR^2$, so $L_C = Mv_{cm}R$.
$L_P = Mv_{cm}R + Mv_{cm}R = 2Mv_{cm}R = 2L_C$. This matches B with IV.

For a solid cylinder, $I_{cm} = \dfrac{1}{2}MR^2$, so $L_C = \dfrac{1}{2}Mv_{cm}R$.
$L_P = \dfrac{1}{2}Mv_{cm}R + Mv_{cm}R = \dfrac{3}{2}Mv_{cm}R = 3L_C$. This matches C with I.

For a solid sphere, $I_{cm} = \dfrac{2}{5}MR^2$, so $L_C = \dfrac{2}{5}Mv_{cm}R$.
$L_P = \dfrac{2}{5}Mv_{cm}R + Mv_{cm}R = \dfrac{7}{5}Mv_{cm}R = \dfrac{7}{2}L_C$. This matches D with III.

Therefore, the correct matching is A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III.

Answer: A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III

questions.q:
The table below gives the initial angular speed, final angular speed, and the time interval for four different wheels subjected to constant angular acceleration.

WheelInitial speed (rpm)Final speed (rpm)Time (s)
A$300$$900$$5$
B$600$$0$$10$
C$1200$$1500$$4$
D$0$$1200$$10$


Which wheel completes exactly $100$ revolutions during its respective time interval?
questions.solution:
For a body undergoing constant angular acceleration, the number of revolutions $N$ can be calculated using the average angular speed:

$N = \text{Average speed in rev/s} \times \text{time in seconds}$

$N = \dfrac{\omega_0 + \omega}{2 \times 60} \times t$

For Wheel A: $N = \dfrac{300 + 900}{120} \times 5 = \dfrac{1200}{120} \times 5 = 50$ revolutions

For Wheel B: $N = \dfrac{600 + 0}{120} \times 10 = \dfrac{600}{120} \times 10 = 50$ revolutions

For Wheel C: $N = \dfrac{1200 + 1500}{120} \times 4 = \dfrac{2700}{120} \times 4 = 90$ revolutions

For Wheel D: $N = \dfrac{0 + 1200}{120} \times 10 = \dfrac{1200}{120} \times 10 = 100$ revolutions

Therefore, Wheel D completes exactly $100$ revolutions.

Answer: Wheel D

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A horizontal uniform circular disc of mass $M$ and radius $R$ is rotating with an angular velocity $\omega_0$ about a frictionless vertical axis passing through its centre. Two small point masses, each of mass $m$, are gently placed at diametrically opposite edges of the disc. What will be the final angular velocity of the system?
questions.solution:
The initial moment of inertia of the disc about its central axis is $I_i = \dfrac{MR^2}{2}$.

When two point masses, each of mass $m$, are placed at the edges (distance $R$ from the axis), the final moment of inertia of the system becomes:
$I_f = \dfrac{MR^2}{2} + 2mR^2 = \left(\dfrac{M}{2} + 2m\right)R^2 = \left(\dfrac{M + 4m}{2}\right)R^2$

Since no external torque acts on the system, the angular momentum is conserved:
$I_i \omega_i = I_f \omega_f$

$\left(\dfrac{MR^2}{2}\right) \omega_0 = \left(\dfrac{M + 4m}{2}\right)R^2 \omega_f$

$\omega_f = \dfrac{M}{M + 4m}\omega_0$

Answer: $\dfrac{M}{M + 4m}\omega_0$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: For a uniform solid cylinder of radius $R$ and length $L$, the radius of gyration about its central geometric axis is equal to its radius of gyration about an axis passing through its centre and perpendicular to its length. The ratio $\dfrac{L}{R}$ is:
questions.solution:
The moment of inertia of a uniform solid cylinder about its central geometric axis is $I_1 = \dfrac{1}{2}MR^2$.
Its radius of gyration about this axis is $K_1 = \sqrt{\dfrac{I_1}{M}} = \dfrac{R}{\sqrt{2}}$.

The moment of inertia of the cylinder about an axis passing through its centre and perpendicular to its length is $I_2 = M\left(\dfrac{R^2}{4} + \dfrac{L^2}{12}\right)$.
Its radius of gyration about this axis is $K_2 = \sqrt{\dfrac{I_2}{M}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{R^2}{4} + \dfrac{L^2}{12}}$.

Given that $K_1 = K_2$, we have:
$K_1^2 = K_2^2$
$\Rightarrow \dfrac{R^2}{2} = \dfrac{R^2}{4} + \dfrac{L^2}{12}$
$\Rightarrow \dfrac{R^2}{2} - \dfrac{R^2}{4} = \dfrac{L^2}{12}$
$\Rightarrow \dfrac{R^2}{4} = \dfrac{L^2}{12}$
$\Rightarrow L^2 = 3R^2$
$\Rightarrow \dfrac{L}{R} = \sqrt{3}$

Answer: $\sqrt{3}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A uniform solid cylinder of mass $M$ and radius $R$ is rolling without slipping on a flat horizontal surface. Let $L_C$ be the magnitude of its angular momentum about its center of mass, and $L_P$ be the magnitude of its angular momentum about a stationary point on the ground. The ratio $\dfrac{L_P}{L_C}$ is :
questions.solution:
For a uniform solid cylinder rolling without slipping with center of mass velocity $v$, its angular velocity is $\omega = \dfrac{v}{R}$.

The moment of inertia of the solid cylinder about its center of mass is $I_{cm} = \dfrac{1}{2}MR^2$.

The angular momentum about the center of mass is:
$L_C = I_{cm}\omega = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}MR^2\right)\left(\dfrac{v}{R}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}MvR$

The angular momentum about a stationary point $P$ on the ground is given by:
$\vec{L}_P = \vec{L}_{cm} + \vec{r}_{cm/P} \times M\vec{v}_{cm}$

Since the cylinder is rolling, the direction of $\vec{L}_{cm}$ and the cross product $\vec{r}_{cm/P} \times M\vec{v}_{cm}$ are the same (both point into the plane of motion). The perpendicular distance from $P$ to the line of motion of the center of mass is $R$.

Thus, the magnitude is:
$L_P = L_C + MvR$
$L_P = \dfrac{1}{2}MvR + MvR = \dfrac{3}{2}MvR$

The ratio is:
$\dfrac{L_P}{L_C} = \dfrac{\dfrac{3}{2}MvR}{\dfrac{1}{2}MvR} = 3$

Answer: $3$

questions.q: A heavy flywheel rotating at $1500\text{ rpm}$ experiences a constant frictional torque. It slows down to $900\text{ rpm}$ in $12\text{ s}$. How much additional time will it take for the flywheel to come to a complete stop?
questions.solution:
Let the constant angular retardation be $\alpha$.

Using the first equation of rotational motion, $\omega = \omega_0 - \alpha t$.

For the first interval:
Initial angular speed, $\omega_0 = 1500\text{ rpm}$
Final angular speed, $\omega = 900\text{ rpm}$
Time, $t = 12\text{ s}$

The rate of decrease of angular speed is:
$\alpha = \dfrac{1500 - 900}{12} = \dfrac{600}{12} = 50\text{ rpm s}^{-1}$.

For the second interval, the flywheel slows down from $900\text{ rpm}$ to rest ($0\text{ rpm}$).
The additional time $t'$ required is:
$t' = \dfrac{900 - 0}{\alpha} = \dfrac{900}{50} = 18\text{ s}$.

Answer: $18\text{ s}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A thin circular ring and a solid cylinder have the same mass and the same radius. The ratio of the radius of gyration of the ring about its central axis to the radius of gyration of the solid cylinder about its central axis is:
questions.solution:
The moment of inertia of a thin circular ring of mass $M$ and radius $R$ about its central axis is $I_{ring} = MR^2$.

The radius of gyration for the ring is $k_{ring} = \sqrt{\dfrac{I_{ring}}{M}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{MR^2}{M}} = R$.

The moment of inertia of a solid cylinder of mass $M$ and radius $R$ about its central axis is $I_{cyl} = \dfrac{1}{2}MR^2$.

The radius of gyration for the solid cylinder is $k_{cyl} = \sqrt{\dfrac{I_{cyl}}{M}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{MR^2}{2M}} = \dfrac{R}{\sqrt{2}}$.

The required ratio is $\dfrac{k_{ring}}{k_{cyl}} = \dfrac{R}{R/\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{1}$, which is $\sqrt{2}:1$.

Answer: $\sqrt{2}:1$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A uniform circular disc has original mass $M$ and radius $R$. A sector corresponding to an angle of $120^{\circ}$ is removed from it. The radius of gyration of the remaining part of the disc about an axis passing through its centre and perpendicular to its plane is:
questions.solution:
The mass of the remaining part of the disc is $m' = \dfrac{360^{\circ} - 120^{\circ}}{360^{\circ}} M = \dfrac{2}{3} M$.

The moment of inertia of a sector of a disc about its central axis is given by $I = \dfrac{1}{2} (\text{mass of sector}) R^2$.

Thus, the moment of inertia of the remaining part is $I' = \dfrac{1}{2} m' R^2$.

The radius of gyration $k$ is defined using the mass of the actual object, so $I' = m' k^2$.

Equating the two expressions for $I'$:
$m' k^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} m' R^2$

$k^2 = \dfrac{R^2}{2} \Rightarrow k = \dfrac{R}{\sqrt{2}}$.

Note that the radius of gyration of a sector of a uniform disc is independent of the angle of the sector and is the same as that of a complete disc.

Answer: $\dfrac{R}{\sqrt{2}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Read the following statements regarding the rotational motion of a system:

(A) If the Earth were to suddenly shrink to half its present radius without any change in mass, the duration of the day would decrease.
(B) The rotational kinetic energy of an isolated collapsing star remains conserved during its contraction.
(C) An ice skater pulling her arms inward decreases her moment of inertia to spin faster.
(D) The angular momentum of an isolated system is conserved only if the net internal force is zero.

How many of the above statements are correct?
questions.solution:
Statement (A) is correct. If the Earth shrinks, its moment of inertia $I$ decreases. By conservation of angular momentum ($L = I\omega = \text{constant}$), its angular velocity $\omega$ must increase. Since the time period $T = \dfrac{2\pi}{\omega}$, the duration of the day decreases.

Statement (B) is incorrect. For an isolated collapsing star, angular momentum $L$ is conserved, but as it contracts, its moment of inertia $I$ decreases. The rotational kinetic energy is given by $K = \dfrac{L^2}{2I}$. Since $I$ decreases, the kinetic energy increases. It is not conserved.

Statement (C) is correct. Bringing mass closer to the axis of rotation decreases the moment of inertia, which by conservation of angular momentum results in a higher angular velocity (spinning faster).

Statement (D) is incorrect. The angular momentum of a system is conserved if the net external torque is zero. Internal forces do not exert any net torque on the system and thus do not affect the conservation of angular momentum, regardless of whether the net internal force is zero or not.

Therefore, exactly two statements (A and C) are correct.

Answer: Two

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A solid cylinder of mass $4 \mathrm{~kg}$ and radius $0.5 \mathrm{~m}$ is rotating about its axis with an angular speed of $20 \mathrm{~rad/s}$. The work required to bring the cylinder to rest is:
questions.solution:
The moment of inertia of a solid cylinder about its axis is given by:
$I = \dfrac{1}{2}MR^2$
$I = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 4 \times (0.5)^2 = 0.5 \mathrm{~kg \cdot m^2}$

According to the work-energy theorem, the work required to stop the cylinder is equal to its initial rotational kinetic energy:
$W = \Delta K = \dfrac{1}{2}I\omega_0^2$
$W = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 0.5 \times (20)^2$
$W = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 0.5 \times 400 = 100 \mathrm{~J}$

Using $I = MR^2$ (as for a ring) would incorrectly give $200 \mathrm{~J}$, and omitting the $\dfrac{1}{2}$ factor in kinetic energy would incorrectly give $200 \mathrm{~J}$ or $400 \mathrm{~J}$.

Answer: $100 \mathrm{~J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A uniform solid cylinder of mass $M$, length $L$ and radius $R$ has the same radius of gyration about its central longitudinal axis as it does about an axis passing through its centre and perpendicular to its length. The ratio of its length to its radius $\left(\dfrac{L}{R}\right)$ is:
questions.solution:
The moment of inertia of a uniform solid cylinder of mass $M$, radius $R$ and length $L$ about its central longitudinal axis is:
$I_{1} = \dfrac{MR^2}{2}$
Its radius of gyration about this axis is $k_{1} = \sqrt{\dfrac{I_{1}}{M}} = \dfrac{R}{\sqrt{2}}$.

The moment of inertia of the same cylinder about an axis passing through its centre and perpendicular to its length is:
$I_{2} = M\left(\dfrac{R^2}{4} + \dfrac{L^2}{12}\right)$
Its radius of gyration about this axis is $k_{2} = \sqrt{\dfrac{R^2}{4} + \dfrac{L^2}{12}}$.

Given that $k_{1} = k_{2}$, we can equate their squares:
$\dfrac{R^2}{2} = \dfrac{R^2}{4} + \dfrac{L^2}{12}$

$\dfrac{R^2}{2} - \dfrac{R^2}{4} = \dfrac{L^2}{12}$

$\dfrac{R^2}{4} = \dfrac{L^2}{12}$

$3R^2 = L^2$

$\dfrac{L^2}{R^2} = 3 \implies \dfrac{L}{R} = \sqrt{3}$

Answer: $\sqrt{3}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A uniform solid cylinder of mass $M$ and radius $R$ is rolling without slipping on a flat horizontal surface. Its centre of mass moves with a constant speed $v$. If $L_C$ is the magnitude of its angular momentum about its centre of mass and $L_P$ is the magnitude of its angular momentum about a stationary point $P$ on the ground, the ratio $\dfrac{L_C}{L_P}$ is:
questions.solution:
For a solid cylinder rolling without slipping, the angular velocity is $\omega = \dfrac{v}{R}$.

The angular momentum about the centre of mass is given by:
$L_C = I_{cm}\omega = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}MR^2\right)\left(\dfrac{v}{R}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}MvR$

The angular momentum about a stationary point $P$ on the ground is the sum of the angular momentum about the centre of mass and the angular momentum of the centre of mass about $P$:
$\vec{L}_P = \vec{L}_C + \vec{r}_{cm} \times M\vec{v}_{cm}$

Since the cylinder is rolling on the ground, the perpendicular distance from $P$ to the line of motion of the centre of mass is $R$. Both the spin and orbital angular momentum vectors point in the same direction.

Thus, the magnitude is:
$L_P = L_C + MvR = \dfrac{1}{2}MvR + MvR = \dfrac{3}{2}MvR$

The required ratio is:
$\dfrac{L_C}{L_P} = \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{2}MvR}{\dfrac{3}{2}MvR} = \dfrac{1}{3}$

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{3}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A solid sphere and a thin hollow sphere have the same mass and the same radius. The ratio of the radius of gyration of the solid sphere to that of the hollow sphere, both calculated about an axis tangent to their respective surfaces, is:
questions.solution:
Using the parallel axis theorem, the moment of inertia of a solid sphere about a tangent axis is:
$I_{solid} = \dfrac{2}{5}MR^2 + MR^2 = \dfrac{7}{5}MR^2$

The radius of gyration of the solid sphere about the tangent is:
$k_{solid} = \sqrt{\dfrac{I_{solid}}{M}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{7}{5}}R$

Similarly, the moment of inertia of a thin hollow sphere about a tangent axis is:
$I_{hollow} = \dfrac{2}{3}MR^2 + MR^2 = \dfrac{5}{3}MR^2$

The radius of gyration of the hollow sphere about the tangent is:
$k_{hollow} = \sqrt{\dfrac{I_{hollow}}{M}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{5}{3}}R$

The required ratio is:
$\dfrac{k_{solid}}{k_{hollow}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{7/5}R}{\sqrt{5/3}R} = \sqrt{\dfrac{7}{5} \times \dfrac{3}{5}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{21}}{5}$

Thus, the ratio is $\sqrt{21}:5$.

Answer: $\sqrt{21}:5$

Answer: $\sqrt{21}:5$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A car accelerates uniformly such that its speed increases from $36$ km/h to $108$ km/h in $10$ s. If the radius of its wheels is $\dfrac{2}{\pi}$ m, how many revolutions does each wheel complete during this time? Assume no slipping.
questions.solution:
Initial linear speed, $u = 36$ km/h = $36 \times \dfrac{5}{18} = 10$ m/s

Final linear speed, $v = 108$ km/h = $108 \times \dfrac{5}{18} = 30$ m/s

Distance covered by the car in $t = 10$ s is given by the average velocity multiplied by time:
$s = \left(\dfrac{u + v}{2}\right) t = \left(\dfrac{10 + 30}{2}\right) \times 10 = 200$ m

In pure rolling, the linear distance covered by the center of mass is equal to the distance rolled by the wheel along its circumference.
Circumference of the wheel, $C = 2\pi R = 2\pi \times \dfrac{2}{\pi} = 4$ m

Number of revolutions completed, $N = \dfrac{s}{C} = \dfrac{200}{4} = 50$

Answer: $50$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two gear wheels, A and B, start from rest and accelerate uniformly. Wheel A attains a rotational speed of $600\text{ rpm}$ in $10\text{ s}$, while wheel B attains a rotational speed of $900\text{ rpm}$ in $12\text{ s}$. The ratio of the angular acceleration of wheel A to that of wheel B is
questions.solution:
Let $\alpha_A$ and $\alpha_B$ be the angular accelerations of wheels A and B respectively.

Since both start from rest, the angular acceleration is given by $\alpha = \dfrac{\Delta\omega}{\Delta t}$.

For wheel A: $\omega_A = 600\text{ rpm}$, $t_A = 10\text{ s}$.
$\alpha_A \propto \dfrac{600}{10} = 60$

For wheel B: $\omega_B = 900\text{ rpm}$, $t_B = 12\text{ s}$.
$\alpha_B \propto \dfrac{900}{12} = 75$

The ratio of their angular accelerations is:
$\dfrac{\alpha_A}{\alpha_B} = \dfrac{60}{75} = \dfrac{4}{5}$.

The conversion factor from $\text{rpm}$ to $\text{rad s}^{-1}$ cancels out in the ratio.

Answer: $4:5$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A uniform solid sphere of mass $M$ and radius $R$ is rotating freely about its diameter with an angular velocity $\omega_0$. Due to internal forces, the sphere contracts uniformly such that its radius becomes $\dfrac{R}{2}$. What is the work done by the internal forces during this contraction?
questions.solution:
The initial moment of inertia of the solid sphere is $I_i = \dfrac{2}{5}MR^2$.

When the radius becomes $\dfrac{R}{2}$, the final moment of inertia is $I_f = \dfrac{2}{5}M\left(\dfrac{R}{2}\right)^2 = \dfrac{1}{4} \left(\dfrac{2}{5}MR^2\right) = \dfrac{I_i}{4}$.

Since there is no external torque acting on the sphere, the angular momentum is conserved:
$I_i \omega_0 = I_f \omega_f$
$I_i \omega_0 = \left(\dfrac{I_i}{4}\right) \omega_f \Rightarrow \omega_f = 4\omega_0$

The initial rotational kinetic energy is:
$K_i = \dfrac{1}{2}I_i\omega_0^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{2}{5}MR^2\right)\omega_0^2 = \dfrac{1}{5}MR^2\omega_0^2$

The final rotational kinetic energy is:
$K_f = \dfrac{1}{2}I_f\omega_f^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{I_i}{4}\right)(4\omega_0)^2 = 4 \left(\dfrac{1}{2}I_i\omega_0^2\right) = 4K_i = \dfrac{4}{5}MR^2\omega_0^2$

According to the work-energy theorem, the work done by the internal forces equals the change in rotational kinetic energy:
$W = \Delta K = K_f - K_i = \dfrac{4}{5}MR^2\omega_0^2 - \dfrac{1}{5}MR^2\omega_0^2 = \dfrac{3}{5}MR^2\omega_0^2$

Answer: $\dfrac{3}{5}MR^2\omega_0^2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A motor rotates with a uniform angular acceleration. It completes $40$ revolutions in $5$ s. If its initial angular speed is $300$ rpm, what is its final angular speed in rpm?
questions.solution:
Initial angular speed, $\omega_0 = 300$ rpm = $\dfrac{300 \times 2\pi}{60} = 10\pi$ rad/s

Angular displacement, $\theta = 40$ revolutions = $40 \times 2\pi = 80\pi$ rad

Using the equation of kinematics for rotational motion:
$\theta = \omega_0 t + \dfrac{1}{2}\alpha t^2$
$80\pi = 10\pi \times 5 + \dfrac{1}{2} \alpha (5)^2$
$80\pi = 50\pi + 12.5 \alpha$
$\alpha = \dfrac{30\pi}{12.5} = 2.4\pi$ rad/s$^2$

Final angular speed, $\omega = \omega_0 + \alpha t$
$\omega = 10\pi + 2.4\pi \times 5 = 22\pi$ rad/s

Converting back to rpm:
Final angular speed = $\dfrac{22\pi \times 60}{2\pi} = 660$ rpm

Answer: $660$

Mass $(m)=2 \mathrm{~kg}$; initial radius of the path
$\left(r_1\right)=0.8 \mathrm{~m}$; initial angular velocity
$\left(\omega_1\right)=44 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{sec}$ and final radius of the path $\left(r_2\right)=1 \mathrm{~m}$
Moment of inertia, $I_1=m r_1^2=2 \times(0.8)^2 =1.28 \mathrm{~kg} \mathrm{~m}^2 and I_2=m r_2^2=2 \times(1)^2=2 \mathrm{~kg} \mathrm{\textrm {m } ^ { 2 }}$
Therefore from the law of conservation of angular momentum $I_1 \omega_1=I_2 \omega_2
or \omega_2=\frac{I_1 \times \omega_1}{I_2}=\frac{1.28 \times 44}{2} \omega_2=28.16 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{sec}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A solid cylinder, a circular disc, a solid sphere and a hollow cylinder of the same radius are placed on an inclined plane. Which of the following will have maximum acceleration at the bottom of the plane?
questions.solution:
Let the inclination of the inclined plane be $\theta$. Acceleration of a rolling body is given as
$a=\frac{g \sin \theta}{\left(1+K^2 / R^2\right)}$ Here, $K$ is radius of gyration. For circular disc $I=\frac{1}{2} M R^2 \quad \therefore \frac{K^2}{R^2}=\frac{1}{2}$ $\therefore \quad a=\frac{2}{3} g \sin \theta$
For solid cylinder $I=\frac{1}{2} M R^2 \therefore \frac{K^2}{R^2}=\frac{1}{2}$ $\therefore \quad a=\frac{2}{3} g \sin \theta$
For solid sphere $I=\frac{2}{5} M R^2 \therefore \frac{K^2}{R^2}=\frac{2}{5}$ $\therefore \quad a=\frac{5}{7} g \sin \theta$
For hollow cylinder $I=M R^2 \quad \therefore \frac{K^2}{R^2}=1$ $\therefore a=\frac{1}{2} g \sin \theta$
Hence, from (i), (ii), (iii) and (iv) we conclude that the solid sphere will reach the bottom with maximum acceleration.

questions.solution: The moment of inertia for a solid sphere along its diameter is I_{$\text{diameter }$}=$\frac{2}{5}$M R² Moment of inertia about a tangent touching to its surface, I_{$\text{tangent }$}=I_{$\text{diameter }$}+M R² (using theorem of parallel axes) =$\frac{2}{5}$M R²+M R²=$\frac{7}{5}$M R²
questions.question: What is the moment of inertia for a solid sphere w.r.t. a tangent touching to its surface?
questions.explanation: The moment of inertia for a solid sphere along its diameter is $$ I_{\text{diameter }}=\frac{2}{5} M R^2 $$ Moment of inertia about a tangent touching to its surface, $$ I_{\text{tangent }}=I_{\text{diameter }}+M R^2 $$ (using theorem of parallel axes) $$ =\frac{2}{5} M R^2+M R^2=\frac{7}{5} M R^2 $$

questions.q: Four holes of radius $R$ are cut from a thin square plate of side $4 R$ and mass $M$. The moment of inertia of the remaining portion about $z$-axis is
questions.solution:
If $M$ is mass of the square plate before cutting the holes, then mass of portion of each hole, $m=\frac{M}{16 R^2} \times \pi R^2=\frac{M \pi}{16}\therefore \quad$ Moment of inertia of remaining portion about $Z$ axis

$\begin{aligned}$& I=I_{$\text{square }$}-4 I_{$\text{hole }$} \\
& =$\frac{M}{12}\left($16 R²+16 R²\right)-4$\left[\frac{m R^2}{2}+$m($\sqrt{2}$R)^2\right] \\
& =$\frac{M}{12} \times$32 R²-10 m R² \\
& =$\frac{8}{3}$M R²-$\frac{10}{16}$M R² $\pi$\\
& I=$\left(\frac{8}{3}-\frac{10 \pi}{16}\right)$M R² .
\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}
& I=I_{\text{square }}-4 I_{\text{hole }} \\
& =\frac{M}{12}\left(16 R^2+16 R^2\right)-4\left[\frac{m R^2}{2}+m(\sqrt{2} R)^2\right] \\

According to law of conservation of angular momentum, when sum of external torques acting on a system is zero, then the total angular momentum of the system remains constant. $\tau=0, L=I \omega=$ Constant
If $I$ increases, $\omega$ decreases and vice versa.

questions.q: If a solid sphere of mass \(1 $\mathrm{~kg}$\) and radius \(0.1 $\mathrm{~m}$\) rolls without slipping at a uniform velocity of \(1 $\mathrm{~m}$/ $\mathrm{s}$\) along a straight line on a horizontal floor, the kinetic energy is
questions.solution:
\(\begin{gathered}
\mathrm{K} . \mathrm{E} \text{ of rolling }=\left(\frac{1}{2} m v^2+\frac{1}{2} I \cdot \frac{v^2}{R^2}\right) \\
\Rightarrow \mathrm{K} \cdot \mathrm{E}=\frac{1}{2} m v^2+\frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{2}{5} \cdot \frac{m R^2 \cdot v^2}{R^2} \\
\mathrm{ K} . \mathrm{E}=\frac{1}{2} m v^2 \times \frac{7}{5} \\
m=1 \mathrm{ kg}, \quad v = 1  m/s \\
\mathrm{ K} \cdot \mathrm{E}=\frac{1}{2} \times 1 \times 1 \times \frac{7}{5}=\frac{7}{10} \mathrm{ J}
\end{gathered}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two masses are attached to a rod end to end. If torque is applied they rotate with angular acceleration $\alpha$. If their distances are doubled and same torque is applied, then they move with angular acceleration
questions.solution: Suppose the masses $m_1$ and $m_2$ are attached to the ends of a massless rod. $C_1$ is the axis of rotation which is at a distance $R$ from each of the masses. $\therefore$ the moment of inertia of the system, $\mathrm{I}=$m_1 R²+m_2 R²=$\left($m_1+m_2\right) R² Now if the distance between the masses is doubled, then the moment of inertia \Gamma=m_1(2 R)^2+m_2(2 R)^2=$\left($m_1+m_2\right) 4 R² Since the same torque is applied in both the cases, $\begin{aligned}$& \tau=I $\alpha=$I^{\prime} $\alpha^{\prime}$\\ & \Rightarrow $\alpha^{\prime}=\frac{I \alpha}{I^{\prime}}=\frac{\left(m_1+m_2\right) R^2 \alpha}{\left(m_1+m_2\right) 4 R^2}=\frac{\alpha}{4} \end{aligned}$
questions.question: Two masses are attached to a rod end to end. If torque is applied they rotate with angular acceleration $\alpha$. If their distances are doubled and same torque is applied, then they move with angular acceleration
questions.explanation: Suppose the masses $m_1$ and $m_2$ are attached to the ends of a massless rod. $C_1$ is the axis of rotation which is at a distance $R$ from each of the masses. $\therefore$ the moment of inertia of the system, $$ \mathrm{I}=m_1 R^2+m_2 R^2=\left(m_1+m_2\right) R^2 $$ Now if the distance between the masses is doubled, then the moment of inertia $$ \Gamma=m_1(2 R)^2+m_2(2 R)^2=\left(m_1+m_2\right) 4 R^2 $$ Since the same torque is applied in both the cases, $$ \begin{aligned} & \tau=I \alpha=I^{\prime} \alpha^{\prime} \\ & \Rightarrow \alpha^{\prime}=\frac{I \alpha}{I^{\prime}}=\frac{\left(m_1+m_2\right) R^2 \alpha}{\left(m_1+m_2\right) 4 R^2}=\frac{\alpha}{4} \end{aligned} $$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two disc having mass ratio $1 / 2$ and diameter ratio $2 / 1$ then find ratio of moment of inertia.
questions.solution:
Given, mass ratio of two disc
$\mathrm{m}_1: \mathrm{m}_2=1: 2 \text{ i.e. } \frac{\mathrm{m}_1}{\mathrm{ m}_2}=\frac{1}{2}$
and diameter ratio $\frac{\mathrm{d}_1}{\mathrm{ d}_2}=\frac{2}{1} \Rightarrow \frac{\mathrm{r}_1}{\mathrm{r}_2}=\frac{2}{1} \therefore$ Ratio of their moment of inertia,
$\begin{array}{ll}
\quad \frac{\mathrm{I}_1}{\mathrm{I}_2}=& \frac{\frac{\mathrm{m}_1 \mathrm{r}_1^2}{2}}{\frac{\mathrm{m}_2 \mathrm{r}_2^2}{2}}=\frac{\mathrm{m}_1}{\mathrm{ m}_2} \cdot\left(\frac{\mathrm{r}_1}{\mathrm{r}_2}\right)^2=\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{2}{1}\right)^2=\frac{2}{1} \\
\therefore \quad \mathrm{I}_1: \mathrm{I}_2=2: 1
\end{array}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Find ratio of radius of gyration of a disk and ring of same radii at their tangential axis in plane.
questions.solution:
For disk, moment of inertia about the diameter, $\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{d}}=\frac{\mathrm{mr}^2}{4}$ and moment of inertia about the tangential axis
$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{I}_{\text{disc }}=\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{d}}+\mathrm{mr}^2 \\ & \mathrm{I}_{\text{disc }}=\frac{\mathrm{mr}^2}{4}+\mathrm{mr}^2 \\ & \mathrm{I}_{\text{disc }}=\frac{5 \mathrm{mr}^2}{4}\end{aligned}$
Let the radius of gyration of disc is $\mathrm{k}_{\text{disc }}$.
$\begin{aligned} \mathrm{I}_{\text{disc }} & =\mathrm{mk}_{\text{disc }}^2 \\ \frac{5 \mathrm{mr}^2}{4} & =\mathrm{mk}_{\text{disc }}^2 \\ \mathrm{k}_{\text{disc }}^2 & =\sqrt{\frac{5}{4} \mathrm{r}}\end{aligned}$
For ring, moment of inertia about the diameter
$\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{a}}^{\prime}=\mathrm{mr}^2 / 2$
and moment of inertia about the tangential axis
$\mathrm{I}_{\text{ring }}=\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{a}}^{\prime}+\mathrm{mr}^2=\frac{\mathrm{mr}^2}{2}+\mathrm{mr}^2=\frac{3}{2} \mathrm{mr}^2$
Let the radius of gyration of ring $\mathrm{k}_{\text{ring }}$.
$\begin{aligned} \mathrm{I}_{\text{ring }} & =\mathrm{mk}^2 \text{ ring } \\ \frac{3}{2} \mathrm{mr}^2 & =\mathrm{mk}^2 \text{ ring } \\ \mathrm{k}_{\text{ring }} & =\sqrt{\frac{3}{2}} \mathrm{r} \\ \frac{\mathrm{k}_{\text{disc }}}{\mathrm{k}_{\text{ring }}} & =\frac{\sqrt{\frac{5}{4} \mathrm{r}}}{\sqrt{\frac{3}{2}} \mathrm{r}}=\sqrt{\frac{5}{6}}\end{aligned}$
questions.question: Find ratio of radius of gyration of a disk and ring of same radii at their tangential axis in plane.
questions.explanation:
For disk, moment of inertia about the diameter, $\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{d}}=\frac{\mathrm{mr}^2}{4}$ and moment of inertia about the tangential axis
$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{I}_{\text{disc }}=\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{d}}+\mathrm{mr}^2 \\ & \mathrm{I}_{\text{disc }}=\frac{\mathrm{mr}^2}{4}+\mathrm{mr}^2 \\ & \mathrm{I}_{\text{disc }}=\frac{5 \mathrm{mr}^2}{4}\end{aligned}$

For ring, moment of inertia about the diameter
$\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{a}}^{\prime}=\mathrm{mr}^2 / 2$
and moment of inertia about the tangential axis
$\mathrm{I}_{\text{ring }}=\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{a}}^{\prime}+\mathrm{mr}^2=\frac{\mathrm{mr}^2}{2}+\mathrm{mr}^2=\frac{3}{2} \mathrm{mr}^2$
Let the radius of gyration of ring $\mathrm{k}_{\text{ring }}$.

questions.q: A uniform rod of mass m and length $l_0$ is pivoted at one end and is hanging in the vertical direction. The period of small angular oscillations of the rod is
questions.solution:
Here, the rod is oscillating about an end point $O$. Hence, moment of inertia of rod about the point of oscillating is
$\mathrm{I}=\frac{1}{3} \mathrm{~m} l_0^2$
Moreover, length $l$ of the pendulum = distance from the oscillation axis to centre of mass of rod
$=l_0 / 2 \therefore$ Time period of oscillation,
$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{T}=2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{I}}{\mathrm{mg} l}}=2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{\frac{\mathrm{l}}{3} \mathrm{~m} l_0^2}{m g\left(\frac{l_0}{2}\right)}} \\ & \Rightarrow \quad \mathrm{T}=2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{2 l_0}{3 \mathrm{~g}}} \\ & \end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A disc of moment of inertia $2 \mathrm{~kg}-\mathrm{m}^2$ revolving with $8 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s}$ is placed on another disc of moment of inertia $4 \mathrm{~kg}-\mathrm{m}^2$ revolving $4 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s}$. What is the angular frequency of composite disc?
questions.solution:
Given that, moment of inertia of discs,
$\mathrm{I}_1=2 \mathrm{~kg}-\mathrm{m}^2, \mathrm{I}_2=4 \mathrm{~kg}-\mathrm{m}^2$
Angular velocity of discs, $\omega_1=8 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s}$, $\omega_2=4 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s}$
From angular momentum conservation principle,
$\mathrm{I}_1 \omega_1+\mathrm{I}_2 \omega_2=\left(\mathrm{I}_1+\mathrm{I}_2\right) \omega$
or $\quad 2 \times 8+4 \times 4=(2+4) \omega$
or $\quad \omega=\frac{16+16}{6}=\frac{32}{6}=\frac{16}{3} \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s}$

$\mathrm{I}_1 \omega_1+\mathrm{I}_2 \omega_2=\left(\mathrm{I}_1+\mathrm{I}_2\right) \omega$
or $\quad 2 \times 8+4 \times 4=(2+4) \omega$
or $\quad \omega=\frac{16+16}{6}=\frac{32}{6}=\frac{16}{3} \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s}$

questions.q: $A B C$ is right angled triangular plane of uniform thickness. The sides are such that $A B \gt B C$ as shown in figure. $I_1, I_2, I_3$ are moments of inertia about $A B, B C$ and $A C$, respectively. Then which of the following relations is correct?
questions.solution:
The moment of inertia of a body about an axis depends not only on the mass of the body but also on the distribution of mass about the axis. For a given body mass is same, so it will depend only on the distribution of mass about the axis. The mass is farthest from axis $B C$, so $I_2$ is maximum mass is nearest to axis $A C$, so $I_3$ is minimum.
Hence, the correct sequence will be $I_2 \gt I_1 \gt I_3$
